units.title: OP Stack chains with ETH gas
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Leads L-769 and L-764. research/network-risk/cycles/015/theme-monad-emitter-blocks.work holds a harness (harness.cpp) that links Monad's interpreter, x86 emitter and runtime from category-labs/monad v0.16.7 and runs the deployed PoolManager code twice from one state, interpreted and native, comparing call results, gas, storage, transient storage, balances and logs. It found no difference on about 2.2 million calls. Its limits: runtime symbols the emitter references were stubbed, the evmc header was the upstream one with the fork's four struct fields added by hand, and asmjit was at commit 9eb6edbf, which was not checked against the release's submodule pin. Task 1: read the submodule pins of category-labs/monad at tags v0.16.7 and v0.16.5 (the .gitmodules file and the tree entries for third_party or equivalent, through raw.githubusercontent.com, cdn.jsdelivr.net or the GitHub API) and name the exact asmjit and evmc commits. Rebuild the harness with those commits and with the real runtime in place of each stub that the PoolManager's code can reach (list every stub and say whether a PoolManager instruction can call it). Rerun the 20,000 scenarios and the nine per-path batteries and report any difference. Task 2: replay mined Monad transactions through the same harness. research/network-risk/cycles/013 holds the mined PoolManager transactions of Monad with their parent-block storage (see the theme-mined-replay and theme-swap-residuals work directories and OPCODES.md, section What cycle 13 added); feed each one to both engines and compare with each other and with the mined receipt (status, gas used by the PoolManager frame where it can be isolated, logs). Task 3: diff the emitter source between v0.16.5 and v0.16.7 (files under category/vm/compiler and category/vm/runtime) and say what changed for the instructions the PoolManager uses. Task 4: the emitter keeps a virtual stack and picks among several code shapes per instruction depending on whether operands are constants, in registers or in memory. For MULMOD, ADDMOD, SDIV, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, BYTE, SHL, SHR, EXP, CALLDATALOAD, MSTORE8, MCOPY, TLOAD and TSTORE, list every shape the emitter can pick, find in the assembly log of the deployed code (pm.asm in the cycle 15 work directory) which shapes the PoolManager's blocks actually use, and for each shape that occurs make sure at least one harness scenario executes it with operands at the edges (zero, one, 2^255, 2^256-1, shift counts of 255, 256 and above, byte index 31 and 32). Report shapes that occur in pm.asm and that no scenario executed.

MegaETH's sequencer is closed (mega-reth/v2.2.3-72527bc). The public stateless validator re-executes blocks from a witness and checks the post-state root; research/network-risk/cycles/015/theme-closed-producers-2.work/svbuild holds a cargo fetch of megaeth-labs/stateless-validator at e1618ed7 with its git dependencies (mega-evm v1.7.3 at 59b8e391, salt, reth v2.3.0), and mega_getBlockWitness on https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc returned a witness for block 32,772,485. The repository pins nightly-2026-04-23, which is not installed, and installing a toolchain is not allowed. Task 1: try to build it with the installed stable toolchain. Read rust-toolchain.toml and the crate attributes to see which unstable features it needs; RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1 lets a stable compiler accept feature gates and is an environment variable, not an installation. Build offline from the fetched sources where possible (CARGO_HOME pointed at the existing cargohome). If the whole validator does not build, build the smallest part that re-executes one block from a witness: mega-evm with revm and the salt state, with a small driver of your own. Report exactly which step fails if none builds. Task 2: with whatever runs, re-execute MegaETH blocks that hold PoolManager liquidity removals (ModifyLiquidity with negative liquidityDelta), fee collections, ERC-6909 burns and mints, and the take calls inside reverted frames that cycle 13 found (the lists are in research/network-risk/cycles/013 and cycles/015/theme-closed-producers-2.work), and compare the post-state root or, failing that, the PoolManager's storage writes and the token transfers with what the sequencer's block holds. Task 3: if nothing builds, do the same comparison with research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py from parent-block state read with eth_getProof or debug_traceTransaction prestateTracer, for at least 300 removals and fee collections, checking every storage word the PoolManager wrote (prestateTracer in diff mode) and every Transfer amount out of the PoolManager against SqrtPriceMath.getAmount0Delta and getAmount1Delta in v4math.py. Task 4: mega-evm changes gas accounting and adds limits (compute gas, data and key-value update limits per transaction and per block). Read mega-evm v1.7.3 and say for each limit what happens to a PoolManager call that hits it inside unlock: does the whole transaction revert, or can one inner frame halt while the outer frames continue with state the source assumes rolled back (src/libraries/Lock.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol, CurrencyDelta.sol)? Test with eth_call and state overrides where a limit can be reached.

Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. A logic property of v4-core met a network feature in cycle 15, and this theme looks for the same meeting on the other networks. The property: PoolManager.sync(currency) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) needs no unlock and records the currency and the PoolManager's balance in transient storage until the end of the transaction; settle (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364) then credits its caller with whatever the balance has grown by since. Inside one transaction, an account whose code runs before and after a third party's token payment to the PoolManager can book that payment as its own. On Ethereum this needs the third party to hand control to the attacker in its own transaction. The network feature found in cycle 15 (finding F-135 in research/network-risk/state/findings.json, read it first): from Tempo's T15 fork a zone portal's processWithdrawals transaction, sent by the zone's sequencer, pays refunds and withdrawals to arbitrary addresses and in the same transaction delivers callbacks to arbitrary contracts. Task 1: for each of the 21 networks in research/network-risk/state/networks.json, list the protocol-level or canonical-bridge transactions that an account other than the beneficiary sends and that (a) can transfer an ERC-20 or the network's token precompile balance to an arbitrary address such as the PoolManager and (b) run code at an address a third account chose, in the same transaction. Candidates to read in source: OP Stack deposit transactions and the L2 cross-domain messenger and standard bridge finalisation (relayMessage), Arbitrum retryable tickets and the L2 gateway router, Polygon state sync and the PoS bridge, BNB Chain's cross-chain and system contracts, Avalanche ICM and Teleporter relays, CCTP v1 and v2 receiveMessage with hooks (lead L-772: has any CCTP message named a PoolManager as mint recipient), Celo's fee currency debit and credit calls around every transaction, Tempo's fee manager, sponsored and batched transactions, the stablecoin DEX and the zone portal, Arc's native USDC precompile and its memo or callback paths, HyperEVM's system transactions from HyperCore, Monad and MegaETH system contracts, and ERC-4337 EntryPoint bundles (handleOps runs many accounts' code in one transaction, and a paymaster or account can pay tokens to any address). For each, say who orders the pieces inside the transaction and whether an ordinary account can place its code on both sides of someone else's payment. Task 2: the same question for payments without a call: balance changes of a pooled token that happen between two frames of one transaction with no transfer call (rebases triggered by an oracle update in the same transaction, system-level mints, fee refunds). Task 3: lead L-771. Read the transfer path of Base's B20 token precompile and of BNB Chain's Jenner CAS20 tokens in the client source the endpoints run. Does either redirect a transfer by a pattern in the recipient address, or call another contract during a transfer? Task 4: for every path found, say whose money the payment is and whether it is lost to its owner without the attacker as well, as in F-135, or whether the bracketing takes money that would otherwise have reached its owner. Only the second kind is a new loss. Report each path as a finding with its actor and the exact preconditions, and report each network where no such transaction exists as cleared with the source read.

Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Lead L-547, widened by the critic of cycle 15. The source relies on a revert rolling back transient storage: the unlock flag (src/libraries/Lock.sol), the count of nonzero deltas (src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol), the per-currency deltas (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol) and the synced reserves (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol). This is tested by simulated calls on all 21 networks and by mined transactions on MegaETH, HyperEVM, Polygon and Monad only. Task 1: on Tempo (4217), Arc (5042), BNB Smart Chain (56), Avalanche (43114), Arbitrum One (42161), Robinhood Chain (4663), Elysium (99901), OP Mainnet (10), Base (8453), Unichain (130) and Celo (42220), find mined transactions in which a call frame into the PoolManager reverted and a later frame of the same transaction called the PoolManager again and succeeded (callTracer over transactions that emitted PoolManager logs; routers that try one path and fall back to another produce these, and so do aggregators that quote by reverting). Use debug_traceTransaction where the endpoint offers it and say where it does not. For each such transaction, rerun it in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py from parent-block state (prestateTracer) and compare the outcome of every PoolManager frame, the logs and the final storage writes. A leaked unlock flag, delta or synced reserve would show as a later frame that succeeds on the chain and fails in the reference, or the other way round. Task 2: the same for frames that halt in other ways than REVERT: out of gas inside a hook or token call with the PoolManager frame catching nothing (it never catches, so the whole unlock reverts; confirm on mined data), invalid opcode, stack overflow at depth 1024, and static-call violation (TSTORE inside STATICCALL). For each halt kind, find or construct with eth_call and state overrides a transaction on each of the 21 networks in which the halting frame had written transient storage before halting, and read the slots afterwards from a later frame with exttload (src/Exttload.sol). Report any network where a halt kind leaves a transient write in place. Task 3: networks with special transaction contexts. For Tempo batched and sponsored transactions, HyperEVM system transactions, OP Stack deposit transactions, Arbitrum retryable redeems, and ERC-4337 bundles on every network, say from client source whether transient storage is cleared between the user operations or calls that the context joins into one transaction, and name a mined transaction in which two unrelated users' PoolManager calls shared one transaction. sync needs no unlock, so a synced currency left by one user is visible to the next in the same transaction: say for each context whether the first user can gain or the second can lose by that (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364, and settle with native value at 353-356).
